overview: The medieval Soninke empire of Ghana prospered through trans-Saharan exchange. Its power rested on commercial connections and political centers such as Kumbi Saleh, rather than a fixed border enclosing one people.

items.text: Gold moved north while salt moved south. Taxing imports and exports helped support imperial rule.
Camel caravans made long desert journeys possible; traders connected different ecological regions rather than transporting goods within a single uniform landscape.
Savanna agriculture and livestock breeding supported the societies through which the trade routes passed.
Al-Bakri described gold-adorned court equipment and clothing. Such written testimony records royal display, not the possessions of every household.
By the late twelfth century Ghana had lost its dominant position in the western Sudan gold trade as routes shifted. Its decline was a process, not a securely dated disappearance of Soninke society.

sources.title: The Met: The Empires of the Western Sudan
